stable.label: Stable
stable.description: Markets function normally. Ore prices steady.
headlines: Markets steady; this column has nothing to add
Ore prices hold as London's traders find little to dispute

article.deck: An unremarkable day on the floor, which this correspondent will take.
article.body:
Orichalchum traded within a narrow band today and closed where it opened. Volumes were ordinary, tempers were ordinary, and the one trader seen shouting was shouting about a parking fine. A man at the Exchange described conditions as "fine", then looked faintly unwell at having said so.

Readers need do nothing. Holdings may be left alone, quotes need not be checked more than twice, and lunch may be taken at lunchtime. Steadiness of this kind rarely lasts, but this column has been wrong about that before, and hopes to be again.

boom.label: Economic Boom
boom.description: Demand up. Buyers flush with cash.
headlines: Buyers flush, demand strong, Exchange in unfamiliar good humour
Boom lifts London's ore trade; caution advised, and ignored

article.deck: Cash is plentiful and buyers are spending it, which this correspondent finds suspicious.
article.body:
Demand for orichalchum and its products rose across the board today, with buyers arriving at the Exchange carrying more cash than sense. Prices firmed by the hour. Even the streets around the Bank were noticeably calmer, there being less need to push what people are happy to pay for.

Traders should sell into strength while it lasts. A man at the Exchange called the mood "sustainable", which in this column's experience is the word used about a month before it is not. Readers who sold early are advised to enjoy it quietly.

recession.label: Recession
headlines: Recession deepens; buyers hold their purses, ore prices soften
As this column warned in the spring, demand has gone

article.deck: Buyers are tight, prices are soft, and the streets are less patient than the markets.
article.body:
Orichalchum fell again today on thin trade, with buyers arriving late, asking questions and leaving without buying. Prices softened across nearly every line. Traders described conditions as "challenging", a word this column has learned to read as "grim".

The cost is not confined to the floor. Where money is short, people take other people's, and incidents of street theft are up on the week. Readers carrying stock should price for patience and carry less of it in public. The warning was given in the spring. It is repeated now at no extra charge.

crisis.label: Financial Crisis
crisis.description: Market collapse. Some ore types in desperate demand.
headlines: Markets suffer "a correction"; Exchange doors remain, for now, open
Financial crisis grips London; one product almost sells out entirely

article.deck: The market has fallen and the streets have noticed. One item alone is in demand.
article.body:
The market suffered what the Exchange is calling a correction, and what everyone outside it is calling something else. Readers may be heartened to hear that quotes only fell in the morning, and dismayed to hear they plummeted after lunch. A man at the Exchange confirmed that "there will be a statement", and was not seen again.

Desperate buyers are paying nearly anything for Be a Lady, whose stock is gone from most shelves. The streets have grown rougher alongside, with muggings sharply up and fewer people willing to walk home with anything worth taking. Readers are advised to hold what they have, keep it close and avoid the Bank after dark. This is unfortunate.

inflation.label: High Inflation
inflation.description: Everything costs more. Daily costs up.
headlines: Prices rise again; the sandwich at Threadneedle Street now requires thought
Inflation bites London: everything costs more, orichalchum included

article.deck: Day-to-day costs are climbing fast, though buyers are, perversely, still buying.
article.body:
Prices rose again across London today, a movement this correspondent can confirm from the sandwich at the café on Threadneedle Street, which now costs what a full lunch used to. Orichalchum moved with the tide, and buyers kept buying, on the theory that anything bought today is cheaper than it will be tomorrow.

The daily cost of living is the real wound. Rent, fuel and food are all climbing faster than anyone's income, and the gap is paid for out of stock or savings. Traders may wish to sell a little more often than they otherwise would.

stable.label: Stable
headlines: Nothing happens in London; reporter checks twice
Quiet day on the streets as the 38 runs to time

article.deck: A calm day citywide, described by this reporter as "suspicious in a nice way".
article.body:
London was quiet today, a finding verified on foot between Bethnal Green and Waterloo. The 38 ran to time. A seller outside the Underground worked his patch at low volume, which observers class as manners. A bun bought at Waterloo was fine.

A close personal source advises that a calm week is for tidying stock, checking locks and doing the washing. The washing has been done. Readers carrying orichalcum or watching veins may wish to see to the other two, as experts are unclear on how long it will stay like this.

unrest.label: Social Unrest
unrest.description: Police busy elsewhere. Raid risks up, but so is opportunity.
headlines: Unrest spreads between boroughs; police "elsewhere"
Bad night in Hackney, though the chip queue held up

article.deck: With police attention stretched, the city is livelier than anyone asked for.
article.body:
Unrest moved through several boroughs overnight, leaving broken windows and one bin found well outside its usual range. Police were largely elsewhere, a position a tired officer described as "operational" and a close personal source translated as "you're on your own, love". The chip shop on the high street stayed open throughout, to general respect.

With attention drawn away, anyone carrying valuables may be of interest to the crews who watch for nights like this. Locks are cheaper than losses. The same source notes that some regard a thin police presence as an opportunity.

lockdown.label: Lockdown
lockdown.description: Movement restricted. Searching harder, yields lower.
headlines: Lockdown notices go up on every lamppost
Everyone indoors, everyone fine, everyone asking about the rent

article.deck: Restrictions on movement make everything slower and the bills a bit steeper.
article.body:
Lockdown notices appeared overnight on lampposts across the city, several of them identical. The instruction is to stay in. One flat visited by this reporter has since established that it can hold a great many snacks.

The wider cost is less cheerful. With the streets shut, searching is slow and finds are smaller: a resident of one building reports four hours out and nothing but a meal deal to show for it. Costs indoors are rising too, from the landlord, the gas and the TV licence. Officials call the measures temporary, somehow while maintaining a straight face. Keep a biscuit in reserve.

festival.label: City Festival
festival.description: Energy high, people out. Physics ore in demand.
headlines: London throws a party, buys all the loud things
City Festival: stilts, flags, and a Wormhole with a ribbon

article.deck: Festival crowds are buying the bangy, shiny and slightly alarming.
article.body:
The City Festival filled the streets with flags and a man on stilts who is a genuine hazard to low-flying traffic. One stall sold a Wormhole, described as "the same as the one in the shop, but with a ribbon". A close personal source bought one. This reporter did not.

Demand is concentrated on Blasts, Shields, Black Holes and, yes, Wormholes, on the principle that nothing says celebration like something that goes off or keeps people away. Traders report brisk business and sore throats. Crowds are in good spirits and guarding their pockets less closely than usual, and anyone out searching for ore has had better luck than usual. Wear sensible shoes.

crime.label: Crime Wave
crime.description: Everyone is at it. Mugging risk elevated.
headlines: Crime wave: everyone is at it, reports Pip, who is not
A close personal source "knows a guy"; the guy is busy

article.deck: Street theft and break-ins are both up, and nobody is sure who is not involved.
article.body:
Six street robberies were reported to this newspaper today before the count was abandoned, partly from fatigue and partly because the reporter had been robbed too, of an umbrella with a duck handle. Its return would be welcomed.

Break-ins are rising alongside. A close personal source says homes are being done with the attention once given to weddings. Anyone with stock at home and no plan to guard it may find someone insistently offering to look after it instead. Readers carrying much of anything should consider where it sleeps. Lock the door, then check the lock.

stable.label: Stable
headlines: Westminster brings no new political pressure to the trade
No new political measure reaches London's calc trade.

article.body: No political shift with a new direct effect on London’s calc trade has been recorded. Market demand, living costs and street risk can still change under the economic and social conditions in force. For now, the political reading adds no further pressure of its own.

war.label: Conflict Abroad
war.description: Military demand. Time and physics ore prices surge.
headlines: Conflict abroad lifts demand for combat supplies
Combat-item demand climbs amid conflict abroad.

article.deck: Buyers seek Shield, Blast, Healing Burst and Black Hole.
article.body: Demand has risen for four finished items used in combat: Shield, Blast, Healing Burst and Black Hole. The change does not set a direct price for the ores used to make them, though shortages and subsequent trade may affect market quotes over time. Mugging risk has also increased during the conflict.

austerity.label: Austerity
austerity.description: Public services cut. Weekly living costs rise; street risk grows.
headlines: Austerity measures raise weekly living costs
Cuts bring a higher weekly bill and more street risk.

article.deck: Households face a higher bill under the latest round of cuts.
article.body: Austerity measures are set to increase weekly living costs across London. The higher bill comes alongside a greater risk of mugging, adding pressure on traders who move stock in person. The change affects household costs and street risk; it does not set the market price of the goods they sell.

regulation.label: Ore Regulation
regulation.description: Government tightens ore controls. Demand for crafted goods rises.
headlines: Ore regulation increases demand for crafted goods
Crafted-item buyers respond to new ore controls.

article.deck: New rules put pressure on the item trade without setting a fixed price.
article.body: The government has announced tighter controls on the ore trade. Demand for crafted goods has risen under the new regulatory climate, although the effect on individual quotes will depend on stock and trading. Dealers are reviewing the rules as they decide what to carry and when to sell.

election.label: Election Period
election.description: Noise and distraction. Barometer effects muted temporarily.
headlines: Election period softens changes in item demand
Election period dampens other item-demand shifts.

article.deck: Campaign activity reduces the force of demand shifts from other conditions.
article.body: The election period is muting changes to crafted-item demand caused by the other active barometer readings. Buyers and sellers will see a smaller demand shift than those conditions would produce on their own.

stancePartner.deck: {first} and {second} make their new partnership public.
stancePartner.body: {first} and {second} have moved into a partnership, recorded on {day}. Both names now appear on the same side of the ledger. Neither faction has said how long the arrangement will last.

stanceHostile.body: {first} and {second} are no longer on speaking terms. The change was recorded on {day}; it raises the temperature between them, but records no raid in itself. Both sides still have people and stock to protect.

veinTaken.deck: A {ore} vein in {district} changes owner after a faction raid.
veinTaken.body: {attacker} has taken a {ore} vein in {district} from {defender}. The transfer was recorded on {day}. {defender} has lost the claim, and {attacker} now holds it. The ore under the street remains where it was.

flood.body: {attacker} has put cut-price {ore} calc into the London market in a move aimed at {defender}. The supply was recorded on {day}. The next quote will also reflect other stock and trades at the daily close.

stockpileRaid.body: {attacker} raided {defender}'s stockpile in {district} and carried off goods. The raid was recorded on {day}. {defender} has moved its remaining stock; no sale or fixed London price follows from the raid alone.

warDeclared.body: {first} and {second} are at war as of {day}. Both factions now have a formal dispute on the books. Any raid or market move that follows will have to stand on its own record.

truceSigned.body: {first} and {second} signed a truce on {day}, set to run until {endDay} unless broken. The agreement clears their current war and queued raids against each other. It does not erase what either side has already lost.

position.deck: A large order for {ore} calc draws attention.
position.body: A buyer took a substantial position in {ore} calc on {day}. The name has not appeared on the public wire. The purchase is recorded in market demand; the next quote will also depend on the rest of the day's trade.
